The early life stages of the Noble pen shell (Pinna nobilis) are characterised by a brief, temperature-sensitive embryonic period. Following external fertilisation, the resulting zygote develops rapidly into a free-swimming trochophore larva. At a water temperature of 21 °C [T = 21 °C], the transition from the embryonated egg to the onset of active, cilia-driven feeding occurs after just 2 days [ab = 2 days]. This remarkably short interval marks the age at birth, when the veliger larva begins to filter-feed on phytoplankton. The initial energy content of a newly formed individual is extraordinarily low, measured at 0.001 J , a value typically associated with the minute, yolk-laden eggs of bivalves. The larval phase continues with a period of planktonic growth and development. The larva reaches a total length of 0.1 cm  at the point of metamorphic competence and subsequent settlement. This morphological transformation, which involves the loss of the velum and the development of the juvenile gill, is a critical bottleneck in the species' life cycle, as it requires a suitable substratum for permanent attachment.

Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a stable 20 °C [T = 20 °C], the entire process from hatching to the completion of larval metamorphosis takes approximately 10 days . This developmental timeline aligns with observations for other large, warm-water pinnid bivalves, although slight variations can occur depending on food availability. The newly settled spat, or post-metamorphic juvenile, begins its benthic existence. Its shell length at this moment of settlement is a mere 0.1 cm , a size that makes it vulnerable to predation and physical disturbance. The transition from a planktotrophic larva to a sessile juvenile represents a profound shift in ecology and energy acquisition. The juvenile will now spend several years growing within seagrass meadows, particularly those of Posidonia oceanica, where it can find stable anchorage and ample suspended organic matter. This early growth phase is characterised by a rapid increase in shell dimensions, leading towards the species' notable ultimate size.

The Noble pen shell is renowned for attaining a particularly large ultimate length in the wild, with a typical maximum size of 86 cm [Li = 86 cm] commonly reported from stable Mediterranean populations. The largest specimen ever documented reached 120 cm, an exceptional size for any bivalve. This impressive growth trajectory is accompanied by a gradual process of sexual maturation. Individuals reach a shell length of 16.5 cm [Lp = 16.5 cm] at the onset of puberty, a measurement that serves as a reliable indicator of reproductive capability in field surveys. This morphological marker of maturity, the total length at puberty, is a key metric for assessing the reproductive potential of a population. The time required to reach this milestone is substantial. The age at puberty since birth, calculated under the stable thermal conditions typical of the species' habitat at 20 °C [T = 20 °C], is approximately 545 days [tp = approximately 545 days]. This period represents the post-larval phase required for an individual to develop its gonads and initiate gametogenesis for the first time.

Field studies have recorded a gonadosomatic index (GSI) of 52% [GSI = 52%] at a water temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], calculated as the weight of the visceral mass, including the gonad, divided by the weight of the total soft tissue. This relatively high index indicates a significant investment of somatic resources into reproductive tissue. Gametes are released during the summer spawning period, with fecundity per reproductive event being extremely high. A large, sexually mature female can release millions of eggs per spawning event, a broadcast-spawning strategy that compensates for high rates of larval mortality. The species typically engages in one or two distinct spawning events during the breeding season, with a reproductive frequency of one to two spawnings per year [F_R_i = one to two spawnings per year]. This pattern of synchronised gamete release maximises the chances of successful external fertilisation in the water column.

The overall lifespan of the Noble pen shell reflects its slow, steady growth and late investment in reproduction. The maximum recorded longevity for this species, determined from mark-recapture studies and analysis of annual growth rings on the shell, is approximately 27 years [am = approximately 27 years] under the typical thermal regime of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. This considerable lifespan allows individuals to reach their full potential in size and to participate in many reproductive seasons over their lifetime, thereby contributing significantly to population recruitment over decades. The initial growth increment, measured as the total length at birth, is incredibly fine, with a newly settled larva measuring just 0.0085 cm [Lb = 0.0085 cm]. This minute size at the point of settlement highlights the extreme vulnerability of early life stages. Conservation efforts for this critically endangered species must therefore consider the protection of its seagrass nursery habitats, ensuring that both juveniles and the long-lived adult population can sustain future generations in the face of ongoing environmental pressures such as habitat loss and the devastating impact of the haplosporidan parasite.
